title: Grade 4 HINDU RELIGIOUS EDUCATION — 5.1 Aspects of integrity

pages.lesson:
PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Sadachaar means good conduct. Integrity is the part of good conduct that stays honest when nobody is clapping. This sub-strand uses moral stories from the four faiths, looks at honesty with money and with technology, and teaches the safe, fair practices of a passenger boarding and leaving a vehicle.

## Strand 5.0: Sadachaar
Sub-strand 5.1: Aspects of integrity
Suggested lessons: 10

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) state the importance of integrity in their daily life for righteous living
b) identify elements of integrity among peers and society for inspiration
c) model elements of integrity for self- efficacy
d) State ideal practices of a passenger during boarding and alighting for safety
e) appreciate the value of integrity by living an exemplary life in class, school and community for harmony

## What this sub-strand covers
• Parables from the four faiths. (Moral stories from the four faiths)
• Practices of a passenger

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why should you practise integrity in life?
2. Which actions do you associate with integrity?
3. How can you use the internet responsibly?

## Core competencies
• Self-efficacy: learner enhances effective communication skills when sharing, in groups, their personal experiences on integrity and performing skits from the parables depicting the value of integrity.
• Digital Literacy: Learner develops digital citizenship skills when demonstrating the value of integrity in using technology responsibly.

## Values
• Integrity: Learner inculcates honesty when demonstrating the value of integrity in using technology responsibly.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Life skills, Values: Learner develops values while creating a lost and found corner for recovered items.
• Education for sustainable development (ESD): Learner enhances financial literacy while discussing the value of integrity in handling money.

## Links to other learning areas
• Learner is able to link the value of integrity in handling money to the skills learnt in Mathematics.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Hindu Religious Education Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 5.0 Sadachaar, Sub-strand 5.1 Aspects of integrity

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: What integrity means

LESSON 1: WHAT INTEGRITY MEANS
==============================

## What you will learn
• Define integrity in simple words.
• State why integrity matters for righteous living.

Curriculum outcomes: a) state the importance of integrity in their daily life for righteous living

## Introduction
A coin left on an empty desk tests a person more clearly than a poster about honesty. Integrity is doing what is right even when no teacher is in the room and even when a lie would be easier.

## Notes
### A working definition
Integrity means being whole and honest. Your words match your actions. You tell the truth, you keep a fair promise, and you do not take what is not yours. People can rely on you when you are watched and when you are not.

Sadachaar, good conduct, is wider than one rule. It includes kindness, cleanliness and respect. Integrity is the backbone of that conduct. Without it, other virtues become a performance.

### Why it matters every day
- A friend who has integrity will not betray a secret for a laugh, and will not promise help and then vanish.
- A class with integrity does not let one learner be blamed for a mess the group made.
- A home with integrity does not need a lock on every cupboard because the people inside choose not to steal.
- A community with integrity can share a water tap, a queue and a market without everybody cheating.

Righteous living is this kind of life. It is not only for saints in old stories. It is for the line at the school shop today.

### What integrity is not
Integrity is not telling a cruel truth just to hurt someone. It is not confessing other people's secrets. It is not boasting, 'I am the honest one,' while you hide your own mistake. It is quiet correctness.

If you fail, integrity also means you admit the failure. A lie told to cover a small fault usually grows into a bigger one. Owning the fault early is a way back.

## Key words
• integrity — being honest and doing right even when no one is watching
• sadachaar — good conduct
• righteous — just, fair and morally right

## Worked examples

### Example 1
You break a cup at home. Nobody saw you. Which action shows integrity?

Working:
1. Hiding the pieces and blaming a sibling is a lie.
2. Telling a parent what happened, and helping to clear the pieces safely, matches word and deed.
3. Integrity includes the moment when nobody is watching.

Answer: Tell a parent the truth and help to clear up safely.

## Activity: Times when nobody is watching
You will need: Exercise book
1. Each learner writes a definition of integrity in one sentence.
2. Share a personal experience, if you wish, of a time you told the truth or of a time you wish you had. Do not name other children in a shaming way.
3. As a class, list four reasons integrity is needed at school.
4. Agree that stories shared in the group stay respectful and are not repeated as gossip.

## Practice
1. What is integrity?
2. Give two reasons integrity matters in daily life.
3. What should you do after a mistake if you want to keep your integrity?

## Summary
• Integrity is honesty that does not depend on an audience.
• It keeps words and actions together.
• Admitting a fault is part of integrity.

### Answers to practice
1. Being honest and doing what is right even when nobody is watching.
2. Any two: people can trust you, nobody is falsely blamed, promises are kept, shared places stay fair.
3. Admit the mistake truthfully and help to put it right.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Parables of integrity from the four faiths

LESSON 2: PARABLES OF INTEGRITY FROM THE FOUR FAITHS
====================================================

## What you will learn
• Retell one moral story of integrity from each of the four faiths.
• Identify the element of integrity in each story.

Curriculum outcomes: a) state the importance of integrity in their daily life for righteous living; b) identify elements of integrity among peers and society for inspiration; e) appreciate the value of integrity by living an exemplary life in class, school and community for harmony

## Introduction
The four faiths do not tell the same story, but each one praises a person who would rather suffer than cheat. These parables are short enough to act and strong enough to remember.

## Notes
### Sanatan: King Harishchandra
King Harishchandra is remembered for refusing to abandon truth. Tradition says his truthfulness was tested until he lost his kingdom and his comfort, yet he would not tell a lie to escape. The test was bitter. The teaching is not that we should seek misery. It is that a right word is worth more than an easy advantage. Learners meet a small form of his test when the truth will cost them a game or a punishment they deserve.

### Jain teaching: not even what looks unwanted
Jain tradition treats asteya, not taking what is not given, as a vow. A parable used with children is simple because the vow itself is simple: a fruit that falls from a neighbour's tree is still the neighbour's unless it is given. A coin on the classroom floor is not a gift to the finder. Integrity here is stopping your hand.

### Buddhist teaching: a good friend does not lie
The Buddha's advice to Sigala, and the Dhammapada's warning against hatred and careless speech, praise truth. A good friend does not flatter you to your face and sell your trust behind your back. Integrity in friendship means your private words and your public words match.

### Sikh story: Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago
Sikh tradition tells that Guru Nanak Dev Ji was invited to a rich man's feast and also ate simple food in the house of a poor carpenter, Bhai Lalo. The rich host, Malik Bhago, was offended. The Guru showed that food earned by honest work is pure, while wealth gained by squeezing the poor is not. The lesson is about how money is earned, not about how fancy the plate looks.

### Elements to name
Truth-telling, not stealing, loyal friendship and honest earning are elements of integrity. You can find them in peers when someone returns a lost item or refuses to cheat. Appreciate the stories by acting them fairly, without turning another faith into a joke.

## Key words
• parable — a short story that teaches a moral lesson
• asteya — not stealing; not taking what is not given

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which story teaches that food bought with cruel profit is not pure, and which faith tells it?

Working:
1. Harishchandra's story is about refusing to lie.
2. The Jain lesson here is about not taking what is not given.
3. Guru Nanak, Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago teach about honest earning. That is a Sikh janamsakhi.

Answer: The story of Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago, from Sikh tradition.

## Activity: Skits from the four parables
You will need: Space to act, Four story cards
1. Each group takes one faith's story: Harishchandra, the ungiven fruit or coin, a friend who refuses to lie, or Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago.
2. Perform a short skit that shows the honest choice. Do not mock the faith.
3. After each skit, the audience names the element of integrity.
4. Help a classmate who needs a line whispered so that they can still take part.

## Practice
1. What is King Harishchandra remembered for?
2. What lesson does the story of Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago teach?
3. A mango falls from a neighbour's tree. What does the Jain teaching of asteya say?

## Summary
• Harishchandra is honoured for truth even when it cost him.
• Jain asteya says do not take what is not given.
• Buddhist teaching praises a friend who does not lie, and Guru Nanak honours food earned honestly.

### Answers to practice
1. He kept to the truth even when a test took away his comfort and kingdom.
2. Food or wealth earned by honest work is pure. Wealth gained by oppressing others is not.
3. It still belongs to the neighbour unless it is given. Do not take it.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Integrity among peers

LESSON 3: INTEGRITY AMONG PEERS
===============================

## What you will learn
• Identify signs of integrity in classmates and in the wider community.
• Model one of those signs during a game.

Curriculum outcomes: b) identify elements of integrity among peers and society for inspiration; c) model elements of integrity for self- efficacy

## Introduction
Integrity is easier to admire in a king than in the person sitting next to you. This lesson looks at ordinary people: a classmate who owns a foul in a game, a shopkeeper who gives the right change, a prefect who does not take a bribe of sweets.

## Notes
### What to look for
Elements of integrity you can actually see:
- Telling the truth when a mistake would have stayed hidden
- Returning a found item
- Refusing to copy or to let others copy in a test
- Keeping a promise about a meeting place or a shared duty
- Admitting a foul in a game instead of arguing
- A community leader, conductor or shopkeeper who does not cheat a child

You are looking for inspiration, not for a chance to gossip. Say 'I noticed Jordan return the pen,' if Jordan agrees the example is kind. Do not announce another person's private fault to the class.

### Modelling it
To model integrity is to be the example on purpose. In a relay, you do not start early. If you are out in a ball game, you leave the court. If the group is one point short, you do not invent a point. Peers learn more from that action than from a lecture.

Self-efficacy here means you trust that you can do the honest thing and still belong. Friends worth keeping will not dump you for being fair.

### When the group wants you to bend
If several people say, 'Everyone cheats,' that sentence is not proof. It is a test. You can answer, 'I will not.' Then play on, or tell the referee. One honest player does not ruin a game. One cheat can.

Appreciate integrity in society by thanking the person who was fair, even if they are only a classmate. Gratitude makes the good example feel worth repeating.

## Key words
• peer — a person of about your own age or level
• model — to show a value by the way you behave

## Worked examples

### Example 1
In a race, Amina starts a step early and wins. Only she knows. What would modelling integrity look like?

Working:
1. The win is not fair if the start was early.
2. She tells the referee and offers to run again or to give up the place.
3. That action teaches the class more than a speech.

Answer: She admits the early start and accepts a fair result.

## Activity: Honesty in a game
You will need: A simple ball or skipping game the teacher chooses
1. Play a short game with one added rule: each learner must call their own faults.
2. After the game, name elements of integrity you saw, without shaming.
3. Write one element you will model tomorrow.
4. If someone with special needs wants a role such as scorekeeper, give them a real role, not a pretend one.

## Practice
1. Name two elements of integrity you might see among classmates.
2. What does it mean to model integrity?
3. Why is 'everyone cheats' a poor reason to cheat?

## Summary
• Integrity in peers shows up in truth, returned property and fair play.
• Modelling means doing the honest thing in public view.
• Do not gossip about other people's faults.

### Answers to practice
1. Any two: telling a hidden truth, returning a found item, refusing to cheat, keeping a promise, admitting a foul.
2. To behave honestly so that others can see what the value looks like.
3. A common fault is still a fault. Integrity means you can refuse even if others do not.

PAGE 5: Lesson 4: Integrity with money

LESSON 4: INTEGRITY WITH MONEY
==============================

## What you will learn
• Explain honest ways to handle money at home and at the school shop.
• Show why a small dishonest gain is still wrong.

Curriculum outcomes: a) state the importance of integrity in their daily life for righteous living; c) model elements of integrity for self- efficacy

## Introduction
Money is a tool for buying what a family needs. It becomes a test of integrity when there is too much change in your hand, or when a price can be hidden from a parent.

## Notes
### Honest handling
- Count change before you leave the shop. If you were given too much, return the extra at once.
- Do not take coins from a parent's bag, a brother's box or the class collection without permission.
- If you are sent to buy something, bring the item and the right balance home. A detour to spend the balance on sweets is a lie in action.
- Keep a simple note if you are trusted with class money: what came in, what was spent, what remains. Mathematics skills help here. The numbers should match the coins.
- Do not cheat a younger child in a swap because you understand prices better than they do.

### Why the small sum matters
People sometimes say a few shillings do not count. Integrity does not have a minimum price. The habit of taking a little is the same habit that takes a lot later. The person who loses the little sum may be another child.

The story of Malik Bhago warns against wealth that grows by hurting others. The story of Harishchandra warns against escaping a hard moment with a lie. Both apply to a shop counter.

### If you are tempted
Move away from an open purse. Ask an adult if you need money for a real reason. If you already took something, put it back and tell the truth. Fear of punishment is normal. Hiding the act usually makes the punishment, and the shame, larger.

A class that discusses money fairly learns financial honesty early: earn, save, spend on what was agreed, and share without showing off.

## Key words
• change — the money returned to you when you pay more than the price
• balance — the amount left after a payment

## Worked examples

### Example 1
You pay for a pencil and the seller gives you change for a larger note than you handed over. What is the honest action?

Working:
1. The extra change is not yours.
2. Returning it at once prevents the seller from losing money.
3. Walking away quickly is a form of taking what is not given.

Answer: Tell the seller and return the extra change immediately.

## Activity: Honest change
You will need: Play money or bottle tops, A price list
1. In pairs, role-play a purchase. One learner is the seller and gives too much change on purpose.
2. The buyer must notice and return the extra.
3. Discuss why integrity in money matters for a family and for a shopkeeper.
4. Write one rule: 'Money that is not mine goes back the same day.'

## Practice
1. What should you do if a shopkeeper gives you too much change?
2. Why is taking a small sum without permission still wrong?
3. How can a simple written record protect class money?

## Summary
• Return extra change and never take money that was not given.
• A small dishonest gain is still a break of integrity.
• Record class money so that the figures match the coins.

### Answers to practice
1. Return the extra money at once.
2. It is still taking what is not yours, and it trains a dishonest habit.
3. It shows what was collected, spent and left, so the amount can be checked honestly.

PAGE 6: Lesson 5: Integrity online and with devices

LESSON 5: INTEGRITY ONLINE AND WITH DEVICES
===========================================

## What you will learn
• State rules for using the internet and other people's devices honestly.
• Explain what to do when online content is unkind or untrue.

Curriculum outcomes: c) model elements of integrity for self- efficacy

## Introduction
A device can help you learn a prayer or find a map. It can also be used to copy, to insult, or to pretend you are someone else. Integrity includes the way your fingers behave on a screen.

## Notes
### Responsible use
- Do not copy homework from a website or from a friend and pretend you wrote it. A search can teach you; it should not do your thinking for you.
- Do not use another person's phone, password or account. A password is a key, not a toy.
- Do not send a message that you would be ashamed to say in front of a parent. Unkind words online are still your words.
- Do not photograph a classmate for a joke, and do not share their picture without permission.
- Do not click 'buy' or give a home address. Tell an adult about any message that asks for money, photos or secrecy.
- If a page is cruel about a faith, leave it and tell the teacher. Do not spread it.

### Digital citizenship
Citizenship here means you are a member of a community even when the community is on a screen. Members do not vandalise, do not steal and do not lie about their names in order to trap someone. A fake name used to harm a classmate is a serious break of integrity.

### When you make a mistake
If you posted something unkind, apologise to the person, remove it if you can, and tell an adult. Deleting it quietly without an apology is only half honest. If someone else is being targeted, do not join in. Show the message to a trusted adult instead of forwarding it.

Technology is a tool. Integrity decides whether the tool builds trust or breaks it.

## Key words
• password — a secret code that opens a device or an account
• digital citizenship — using technology in a way that is honest and fair to other people

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A classmate's homework is visible on a shared tablet. You could copy it before they return. What does integrity require?

Working:
1. The work belongs to the classmate.
2. Copying it is both stealing and lying.
3. You look away, or you close the screen, and you do your own work.

Answer: Do not read or copy their work. Complete your own.

## Activity: Honest and dishonest uses of a device
You will need: Two columns on the board, Example cards
1. Sort example cards into honest use and dishonest use. Include copying work, asking a parent before a download, sharing a cruel post, and using a map with the teacher.
2. Discuss how integrity guides the honest column.
3. Write three personal rules for devices.
4. Role-play telling an adult about a message that asks you to keep a secret.

## Practice
1. Why is copying an essay from the internet a failure of integrity?
2. What should you do if a message asks you for a photo and tells you not to tell your parents?
3. Name one honest way to use a digital device for learning.

## Summary
• Do not copy, do not use another person's password, and do not send unkind messages.
• Tell an adult about requests for money, photos or secrecy.
• Online words count as much as spoken words.

### Answers to practice
1. You are pretending that someone else's words are your own.
2. Do not send the photo. Tell a parent or teacher at once.
3. Any one: watch a lesson the teacher chose, find a map with an adult, or type your own sentences.

PAGE 7: Lesson 6: A lost and found corner

LESSON 6: A LOST AND FOUND CORNER
=================================

## What you will learn
• Explain how a lost and found corner supports integrity.
• Practise receiving and returning an item fairly.

Curriculum outcomes: c) model elements of integrity for self- efficacy; e) appreciate the value of integrity by living an exemplary life in class, school and community for harmony

## Introduction
A sweater on the field has an owner even if the owner is in another class. A lost and found corner gives integrity a place to go, so that a found item is not stuffed into a desk and forgotten.

## Notes
### How the corner works
Choose a desk, box or shelf that the whole school can understand. A found item is placed there the same day, or handed to the teacher on duty. Money should go straight to a teacher, not into an open box. Valuable items such as watches or spectacles should also go to an adult at once.

The owner describes the item before taking it. This stops a greedy person from claiming everything. Write a simple list if the teacher asks: date, item, who found it, who collected it. The list itself must be honest.

### Your part
If you find a pencil, a bottle or a jumper, you do not keep it because 'finders keepers' sounds catchy. That saying is not sadachaar. Pick the item up, ask nearby if someone just dropped it, and if not, take it to the corner or the teacher.

If you lose something, check the corner before accusing a classmate of theft. False accusations also break integrity.

### An exemplary class
A class becomes exemplary when this habit is normal. Younger learners copy what they see. If Grade 4 learners return items, they teach the school without a long speech. Include everyone: a learner who cannot walk to the field can still record items at the desk.

Harmony grows when people trust that their property is safe. Trust is the fruit of many small honest acts.

## Key words
• lost and found — a place where found items are kept until the owner collects them
• exemplary — good enough to be an example for others

## Worked examples

### Example 1
You find a named water bottle after games. A friend says, 'It has no name I recognise; let us use it.' What should you do?

Working:
1. A bottle someone carried to school is not abandoned treasure.
2. Take it to the lost and found or the teacher.
3. Using it yourself breaks asteya and school trust.

Answer: Hand the bottle to the teacher or place it in the lost and found corner.

## Activity: Set up a lost and found corner
You will need: A labelled box or desk, Paper for a record
1. With the teacher, choose a safe corner and make a clear label.
2. Role-play finding a book, recording it, and returning it only when the owner describes it.
3. Agree special rules: money and valuable items go to an adult immediately.
4. Teach the rules to another group, including any classmate who needs the steps repeated slowly.

## Practice
1. What should you do with a sweater you find on the field?
2. Why should found money not be left in an open box?
3. Why is it wrong to accuse a classmate of stealing before you check the lost and found?

## Summary
• Found items go to a lost and found corner or to a teacher.
• Money and valuable items go straight to an adult.
• A class that returns property becomes an example for the school.

### Answers to practice
1. Ask nearby if it was just dropped, and if not, take it to the lost and found corner or a teacher.
2. Money is easily taken. An adult should receive it so that it can be returned honestly.
3. The item may simply be lost, and a false accusation is unjust.

PAGE 8: Lesson 7: Practices of a passenger

LESSON 7: PRACTICES OF A PASSENGER
==================================

## What you will learn
• State safe ways to board and alight from a vehicle.
• Explain how integrity appears in the way a passenger behaves.

Curriculum outcomes: d) State ideal practices of a passenger during boarding and alighting for safety

## Introduction
A vehicle that is still moving is not a playground. Boarding and alighting are moments when carelessness causes real injury. Good passengers are also honest passengers: they pay, they queue, and they do not shove a smaller child aside.

## Notes
### Before you board
- Wait until the vehicle has fully stopped.
- Queue. Do not push, and do not climb through a window.
- Let a younger child, an older person or a person who needs help board without being crushed. Help a classmate with special needs if they ask or if a teacher asks you.
- Have your fare ready if you are paying. Do not pretend you have already paid.
- Do not board a vehicle a parent has not allowed, and do not go with a stranger who offers a free ride.

### While you are inside
- Sit properly. Do not stand on the seat or lean out of the door.
- Keep hands, head and any sticks inside.
- Do not distract the driver with shouts or by grabbing the steering area.
- Give a seat to someone who needs it more if you can stand safely, and do not spread bags over empty seats while people are standing.
- Do not drop litter or damage the fittings. The vehicle is not yours to spoil.

### Alighting
- Wait until the vehicle stops.
- Use the door. Do not jump.
- Step away from the road, not into traffic.
- Check that a younger sibling is with you before the vehicle moves off.
- If your stop is missed, speak calmly to the conductor. Do not pull at the driver.

### Integrity on the journey
Paying the correct fare, not using a forged excuse, and not destroying property are integrity. Safety rules are integrity too, because showing off at the door risks other people's bodies. A passenger who keeps these practices protects the whole vehicle.

## Key words
• board — to get onto a vehicle
• alight — to get off a vehicle
• fare — the money paid for the journey

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The bus is still rolling when friends start to jump off so they can be first at the gate. What are the safe and honest actions?

Working:
1. Alight only after the bus stops.
2. Use the door and move away from traffic.
3. Pushing to be first risks a fall and is unfair to smaller learners.

Answer: Wait for the stop, use the door, and walk clear of the road without pushing.

## Activity: Passenger checklist
You will need: Paper, A few chairs set in a row to represent seats
1. In groups, prepare a list of ideal practices for boarding and for alighting. Include safety and fair behaviour.
2. Act the correct way, then pause and point out a dangerous mistake such as jumping from a moving vehicle.
3. Add one rule about helping a passenger who needs more time.
4. Post the list in the classroom and read it before the next school trip.

## Practice
1. When is it safe to board or alight?
2. Name two dangerous passenger habits.
3. How does paying the correct fare show integrity?

## Summary
• Board and alight only when the vehicle has stopped.
• Queue, pay the fare, and do not lean out or distract the driver.
• Help passengers who need more time, and keep clear of traffic.

### Answers to practice
1. Only after the vehicle has completely stopped.
2. Any two: jumping off a moving vehicle, leaning out, distracting the driver, pushing in the queue, climbing through the window.
3. You are not cheating the conductor or taking a journey you have not paid for.

PAGE 9: Lesson 8: An exemplary life at school and beyond

LESSON 8: AN EXEMPLARY LIFE AT SCHOOL AND BEYOND
================================================

## What you will learn
• Plan how to practise integrity in class, at school and in the community.
• Appreciate integrity by encouraging others without pride.

Curriculum outcomes: c) model elements of integrity for self- efficacy; e) appreciate the value of integrity by living an exemplary life in class, school and community for harmony

## Introduction
One honest act is good. A life of integrity is a pattern that classmates can recognise over weeks. This last lesson turns the stories, the money rules, the device rules and the passenger rules into a way of belonging with other people.

## Notes
### In class
Do your own work. If you do not know an answer, say so and ask. Do not hide a group mistake inside one quiet person's name. Share materials you were given for everyone. When you mark a friend's book, mark what is truly there.

### In the wider school
Use the lost and found corner. Play games fairly. Speak about other faiths, including your own, without lies or mockery. If you are chosen as a leader, do not take food or money meant for the class. Leadership is a test of integrity, not a prize of extra power.

### In the community
Queue for water or for a vehicle. Return extra change. Point out a danger instead of daring a younger child to try it. If an adult asks you to lie for them, tell a trusted teacher or parent. A child is not required to join someone else's dishonesty.

### Harmony
The outcome of all this is harmony: people can relax because they are not waiting to be cheated. Harmony is not the silence of fear. It is the peace of fair treatment. Stories of Harishchandra, of asteya, of truthful friends and of Bhai Lalo all aim at that peace.

### Without pride
An exemplary learner does not announce, 'I am better than all of you.' Pride spoils the example. If someone fails, help them start again. If you fail, begin again the same day. Write a short essay at home: one story from a faith, one element of integrity, and one habit you will keep. That essay is a promise you can actually fulfil.

## Key words
• harmony — living together in fairness and peace
• habit — an action repeated until it becomes part of your character

## Worked examples

### Example 1
You are the class monitor. Two friends ask you to ignore their copied homework. What keeps both integrity and friendship healthy?

Working:
1. Ignoring the copy would misuse the monitor's trust.
2. You can refuse without insulting them.
3. They should redo the work. You can explain the lesson later if they ask.

Answer: Refuse to ignore the copying, speak respectfully, and let the true work be done.

## Activity: Essay on one habit of integrity
You will need: Exercise book
1. Choose one parable from the four faiths and one element of integrity it teaches.
2. Write a short essay linking that element to class, school or community.
3. Read a few essays aloud. Thank each reader.
4. Peer-teach the main lesson of your parable to a classmate who needs it repeated.

## Practice
1. Give one example of integrity in the classroom and one in the community.
2. Why does pride weaken an otherwise good example?
3. What is the link between integrity and harmony?

## Summary
• Integrity at school means honest work, fair leadership and returned property.
• Integrity in the community means fair queues, honest money and safe choices.
• The aim is harmony, practised without pride.

### Answers to practice
1. Class: doing your own work or not blaming the wrong person. Community: returning extra change, queueing fairly, or not lying for someone.
2. Boasting turns honesty into a performance and can shame other people instead of helping them.
3. When people tell the truth and do not cheat, others can trust them, and life together becomes more peaceful.
pages.quiz:
REVISION QUIZ — 5.1 ASPECTS OF INTEGRITY
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Integrity means
   A. Doing right only when a teacher is watching
   B. Being honest even when nobody is watching
   C. Winning every game
   D. Never admitting a mistake

2. King Harishchandra is remembered because he
   A. Refused to abandon the truth
   B. Taught passengers to jump from buses
   C. Compiled the Guru Granth Sahib
   D. Hid his mistakes

3. The story of Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago teaches that
   A. Rich food is always better
   B. Honest earning is pure, and wealth gained by oppressing others is not
   C. Children should not work
   D. Only carpenters may cook

4. Which action shows integrity among peers?
   A. Admitting a foul in a game
   B. Hiding a group's mistake on a quiet classmate
   C. Copying a test
   D. Keeping a found watch in your bag

5. A shopkeeper gives you too much change. You should
   A. Run before they notice
   B. Return the extra at once
   C. Share it as a gift to friends
   D. Hide it at home

6. Which use of a device shows integrity?
   A. Copying an essay and putting your name on it
   B. Using a friend's password
   C. Typing your own work and telling an adult about a cruel message
   D. Posting a classmate's photo as a joke

7. A found pencil should be
   A. Kept because of 'finders keepers'
   B. Taken to the lost and found or a teacher
   C. Thrown away
   D. Sold

8. When should a passenger alight?
   A. While the vehicle is still moving, if they are late
   B. Only after the vehicle has stopped, using the door and moving clear of traffic
   C. Through the window
   D. Whenever friends start to push

9. Paying the correct fare shows integrity because

10. An exemplary learner practises integrity in order to
   A. Boast that they are better than everyone
   B. Build trust and harmony at school and in the community
   C. Avoid every kind of work
   D. Hide other people's property
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 5.1 ASPECTS OF INTEGRITY
========================================

1. B. Being honest even when nobody is watching
   Integrity is honesty that does not depend on an audience.

2. A. Refused to abandon the truth
   His parable is about truthfulness under severe testing.

3. B. Honest earning is pure, and wealth gained by oppressing others is not
   Guru Nanak contrasted honest work with cruel profit.

4. A. Admitting a foul in a game
   Owning a fault is an element of integrity classmates can see.

5. B. Return the extra at once
   Extra change is not yours. Integrity returns it.

6. C. Typing your own work and telling an adult about a cruel message
   Honest work and reporting harm are responsible digital citizenship.

7. B. Taken to the lost and found or a teacher
   A lost and found corner helps property return to the owner.

8. B. Only after the vehicle has stopped, using the door and moving clear of traffic
   Boarding and alighting safely means waiting for a full stop.

9. You are not cheating the conductor or taking a journey you have not paid for.
   Honesty with the fare is part of a passenger's good conduct.

10. B. Build trust and harmony at school and in the community
   The aim is a trustworthy life, not pride.

studyPages.title: Overview
studyPages.body:
OVERVIEW
========

Sadachaar means good conduct. Integrity is the part of good conduct that stays honest when nobody is clapping. This sub-strand uses moral stories from the four faiths, looks at honesty with money and with technology, and teaches the safe, fair practices of a passenger boarding and leaving a vehicle.

## Strand 5.0: Sadachaar
Sub-strand 5.1: Aspects of integrity
Suggested lessons: 10

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) state the importance of integrity in their daily life for righteous living
b) identify elements of integrity among peers and society for inspiration
c) model elements of integrity for self- efficacy
d) State ideal practices of a passenger during boarding and alighting for safety
e) appreciate the value of integrity by living an exemplary life in class, school and community for harmony

## What this sub-strand covers
• Parables from the four faiths. (Moral stories from the four faiths)
• Practices of a passenger

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why should you practise integrity in life?
2. Which actions do you associate with integrity?
3. How can you use the internet responsibly?

## Core competencies
• Self-efficacy: learner enhances effective communication skills when sharing, in groups, their personal experiences on integrity and performing skits from the parables depicting the value of integrity.
• Digital Literacy: Learner develops digital citizenship skills when demonstrating the value of integrity in using technology responsibly.

## Values
• Integrity: Learner inculcates honesty when demonstrating the value of integrity in using technology responsibly.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Life skills, Values: Learner develops values while creating a lost and found corner for recovered items.
• Education for sustainable development (ESD): Learner enhances financial literacy while discussing the value of integrity in handling money.

## Links to other learning areas
• Learner is able to link the value of integrity in handling money to the skills learnt in Mathematics.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Hindu Religious Education Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 5.0 Sadachaar, Sub-strand 5.1 Aspects of integrity

studyPages.title: Lesson 1: What integrity means
studyPages.body:
LESSON 1: WHAT INTEGRITY MEANS
==============================

## What you will learn
• Define integrity in simple words.
• State why integrity matters for righteous living.

Curriculum outcomes: a) state the importance of integrity in their daily life for righteous living

## Introduction
A coin left on an empty desk tests a person more clearly than a poster about honesty. Integrity is doing what is right even when no teacher is in the room and even when a lie would be easier.

## Notes
### A working definition
Integrity means being whole and honest. Your words match your actions. You tell the truth, you keep a fair promise, and you do not take what is not yours. People can rely on you when you are watched and when you are not.

Sadachaar, good conduct, is wider than one rule. It includes kindness, cleanliness and respect. Integrity is the backbone of that conduct. Without it, other virtues become a performance.

### Why it matters every day
- A friend who has integrity will not betray a secret for a laugh, and will not promise help and then vanish.
- A class with integrity does not let one learner be blamed for a mess the group made.
- A home with integrity does not need a lock on every cupboard because the people inside choose not to steal.
- A community with integrity can share a water tap, a queue and a market without everybody cheating.

Righteous living is this kind of life. It is not only for saints in old stories. It is for the line at the school shop today.

### What integrity is not
Integrity is not telling a cruel truth just to hurt someone. It is not confessing other people's secrets. It is not boasting, 'I am the honest one,' while you hide your own mistake. It is quiet correctness.

If you fail, integrity also means you admit the failure. A lie told to cover a small fault usually grows into a bigger one. Owning the fault early is a way back.

## Key words
• integrity — being honest and doing right even when no one is watching
• sadachaar — good conduct
• righteous — just, fair and morally right

## Worked examples

### Example 1
You break a cup at home. Nobody saw you. Which action shows integrity?

Working:
1. Hiding the pieces and blaming a sibling is a lie.
2. Telling a parent what happened, and helping to clear the pieces safely, matches word and deed.
3. Integrity includes the moment when nobody is watching.

Answer: Tell a parent the truth and help to clear up safely.

## Activity: Times when nobody is watching
You will need: Exercise book
1. Each learner writes a definition of integrity in one sentence.
2. Share a personal experience, if you wish, of a time you told the truth or of a time you wish you had. Do not name other children in a shaming way.
3. As a class, list four reasons integrity is needed at school.
4. Agree that stories shared in the group stay respectful and are not repeated as gossip.

## Practice
1. What is integrity?
2. Give two reasons integrity matters in daily life.
3. What should you do after a mistake if you want to keep your integrity?

## Summary
• Integrity is honesty that does not depend on an audience.
• It keeps words and actions together.
• Admitting a fault is part of integrity.

### Answers to practice
1. Being honest and doing what is right even when nobody is watching.
2. Any two: people can trust you, nobody is falsely blamed, promises are kept, shared places stay fair.
3. Admit the mistake truthfully and help to put it right.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Parables of integrity from the four faiths
studyPages.body:
LESSON 2: PARABLES OF INTEGRITY FROM THE FOUR FAITHS
====================================================

## What you will learn
• Retell one moral story of integrity from each of the four faiths.
• Identify the element of integrity in each story.

Curriculum outcomes: a) state the importance of integrity in their daily life for righteous living; b) identify elements of integrity among peers and society for inspiration; e) appreciate the value of integrity by living an exemplary life in class, school and community for harmony

## Introduction
The four faiths do not tell the same story, but each one praises a person who would rather suffer than cheat. These parables are short enough to act and strong enough to remember.

## Notes
### Sanatan: King Harishchandra
King Harishchandra is remembered for refusing to abandon truth. Tradition says his truthfulness was tested until he lost his kingdom and his comfort, yet he would not tell a lie to escape. The test was bitter. The teaching is not that we should seek misery. It is that a right word is worth more than an easy advantage. Learners meet a small form of his test when the truth will cost them a game or a punishment they deserve.

### Jain teaching: not even what looks unwanted
Jain tradition treats asteya, not taking what is not given, as a vow. A parable used with children is simple because the vow itself is simple: a fruit that falls from a neighbour's tree is still the neighbour's unless it is given. A coin on the classroom floor is not a gift to the finder. Integrity here is stopping your hand.

### Buddhist teaching: a good friend does not lie
The Buddha's advice to Sigala, and the Dhammapada's warning against hatred and careless speech, praise truth. A good friend does not flatter you to your face and sell your trust behind your back. Integrity in friendship means your private words and your public words match.

### Sikh story: Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago
Sikh tradition tells that Guru Nanak Dev Ji was invited to a rich man's feast and also ate simple food in the house of a poor carpenter, Bhai Lalo. The rich host, Malik Bhago, was offended. The Guru showed that food earned by honest work is pure, while wealth gained by squeezing the poor is not. The lesson is about how money is earned, not about how fancy the plate looks.

### Elements to name
Truth-telling, not stealing, loyal friendship and honest earning are elements of integrity. You can find them in peers when someone returns a lost item or refuses to cheat. Appreciate the stories by acting them fairly, without turning another faith into a joke.

## Key words
• parable — a short story that teaches a moral lesson
• asteya — not stealing; not taking what is not given

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which story teaches that food bought with cruel profit is not pure, and which faith tells it?

Working:
1. Harishchandra's story is about refusing to lie.
2. The Jain lesson here is about not taking what is not given.
3. Guru Nanak, Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago teach about honest earning. That is a Sikh janamsakhi.

Answer: The story of Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago, from Sikh tradition.

## Activity: Skits from the four parables
You will need: Space to act, Four story cards
1. Each group takes one faith's story: Harishchandra, the ungiven fruit or coin, a friend who refuses to lie, or Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago.
2. Perform a short skit that shows the honest choice. Do not mock the faith.
3. After each skit, the audience names the element of integrity.
4. Help a classmate who needs a line whispered so that they can still take part.

## Practice
1. What is King Harishchandra remembered for?
2. What lesson does the story of Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago teach?
3. A mango falls from a neighbour's tree. What does the Jain teaching of asteya say?

## Summary
• Harishchandra is honoured for truth even when it cost him.
• Jain asteya says do not take what is not given.
• Buddhist teaching praises a friend who does not lie, and Guru Nanak honours food earned honestly.

### Answers to practice
1. He kept to the truth even when a test took away his comfort and kingdom.
2. Food or wealth earned by honest work is pure. Wealth gained by oppressing others is not.
3. It still belongs to the neighbour unless it is given. Do not take it.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Integrity among peers
studyPages.body:
LESSON 3: INTEGRITY AMONG PEERS
===============================

## What you will learn
• Identify signs of integrity in classmates and in the wider community.
• Model one of those signs during a game.

Curriculum outcomes: b) identify elements of integrity among peers and society for inspiration; c) model elements of integrity for self- efficacy

## Introduction
Integrity is easier to admire in a king than in the person sitting next to you. This lesson looks at ordinary people: a classmate who owns a foul in a game, a shopkeeper who gives the right change, a prefect who does not take a bribe of sweets.

## Notes
### What to look for
Elements of integrity you can actually see:
- Telling the truth when a mistake would have stayed hidden
- Returning a found item
- Refusing to copy or to let others copy in a test
- Keeping a promise about a meeting place or a shared duty
- Admitting a foul in a game instead of arguing
- A community leader, conductor or shopkeeper who does not cheat a child

You are looking for inspiration, not for a chance to gossip. Say 'I noticed Jordan return the pen,' if Jordan agrees the example is kind. Do not announce another person's private fault to the class.

### Modelling it
To model integrity is to be the example on purpose. In a relay, you do not start early. If you are out in a ball game, you leave the court. If the group is one point short, you do not invent a point. Peers learn more from that action than from a lecture.

Self-efficacy here means you trust that you can do the honest thing and still belong. Friends worth keeping will not dump you for being fair.

### When the group wants you to bend
If several people say, 'Everyone cheats,' that sentence is not proof. It is a test. You can answer, 'I will not.' Then play on, or tell the referee. One honest player does not ruin a game. One cheat can.

Appreciate integrity in society by thanking the person who was fair, even if they are only a classmate. Gratitude makes the good example feel worth repeating.

## Key words
• peer — a person of about your own age or level
• model — to show a value by the way you behave

## Worked examples

### Example 1
In a race, Amina starts a step early and wins. Only she knows. What would modelling integrity look like?

Working:
1. The win is not fair if the start was early.
2. She tells the referee and offers to run again or to give up the place.
3. That action teaches the class more than a speech.

Answer: She admits the early start and accepts a fair result.

## Activity: Honesty in a game
You will need: A simple ball or skipping game the teacher chooses
1. Play a short game with one added rule: each learner must call their own faults.
2. After the game, name elements of integrity you saw, without shaming.
3. Write one element you will model tomorrow.
4. If someone with special needs wants a role such as scorekeeper, give them a real role, not a pretend one.

## Practice
1. Name two elements of integrity you might see among classmates.
2. What does it mean to model integrity?
3. Why is 'everyone cheats' a poor reason to cheat?

## Summary
• Integrity in peers shows up in truth, returned property and fair play.
• Modelling means doing the honest thing in public view.
• Do not gossip about other people's faults.

### Answers to practice
1. Any two: telling a hidden truth, returning a found item, refusing to cheat, keeping a promise, admitting a foul.
2. To behave honestly so that others can see what the value looks like.
3. A common fault is still a fault. Integrity means you can refuse even if others do not.

studyPages.title: Lesson 4: Integrity with money
studyPages.body:
LESSON 4: INTEGRITY WITH MONEY
==============================

## What you will learn
• Explain honest ways to handle money at home and at the school shop.
• Show why a small dishonest gain is still wrong.

Curriculum outcomes: a) state the importance of integrity in their daily life for righteous living; c) model elements of integrity for self- efficacy

## Introduction
Money is a tool for buying what a family needs. It becomes a test of integrity when there is too much change in your hand, or when a price can be hidden from a parent.

## Notes
### Honest handling
- Count change before you leave the shop. If you were given too much, return the extra at once.
- Do not take coins from a parent's bag, a brother's box or the class collection without permission.
- If you are sent to buy something, bring the item and the right balance home. A detour to spend the balance on sweets is a lie in action.
- Keep a simple note if you are trusted with class money: what came in, what was spent, what remains. Mathematics skills help here. The numbers should match the coins.
- Do not cheat a younger child in a swap because you understand prices better than they do.

### Why the small sum matters
People sometimes say a few shillings do not count. Integrity does not have a minimum price. The habit of taking a little is the same habit that takes a lot later. The person who loses the little sum may be another child.

The story of Malik Bhago warns against wealth that grows by hurting others. The story of Harishchandra warns against escaping a hard moment with a lie. Both apply to a shop counter.

### If you are tempted
Move away from an open purse. Ask an adult if you need money for a real reason. If you already took something, put it back and tell the truth. Fear of punishment is normal. Hiding the act usually makes the punishment, and the shame, larger.

A class that discusses money fairly learns financial honesty early: earn, save, spend on what was agreed, and share without showing off.

## Key words
• change — the money returned to you when you pay more than the price
• balance — the amount left after a payment

## Worked examples

### Example 1
You pay for a pencil and the seller gives you change for a larger note than you handed over. What is the honest action?

Working:
1. The extra change is not yours.
2. Returning it at once prevents the seller from losing money.
3. Walking away quickly is a form of taking what is not given.

Answer: Tell the seller and return the extra change immediately.

## Activity: Honest change
You will need: Play money or bottle tops, A price list
1. In pairs, role-play a purchase. One learner is the seller and gives too much change on purpose.
2. The buyer must notice and return the extra.
3. Discuss why integrity in money matters for a family and for a shopkeeper.
4. Write one rule: 'Money that is not mine goes back the same day.'

## Practice
1. What should you do if a shopkeeper gives you too much change?
2. Why is taking a small sum without permission still wrong?
3. How can a simple written record protect class money?

## Summary
• Return extra change and never take money that was not given.
• A small dishonest gain is still a break of integrity.
• Record class money so that the figures match the coins.

### Answers to practice
1. Return the extra money at once.
2. It is still taking what is not yours, and it trains a dishonest habit.
3. It shows what was collected, spent and left, so the amount can be checked honestly.

studyPages.title: Lesson 5: Integrity online and with devices
studyPages.body:
LESSON 5: INTEGRITY ONLINE AND WITH DEVICES
===========================================

## What you will learn
• State rules for using the internet and other people's devices honestly.
• Explain what to do when online content is unkind or untrue.

Curriculum outcomes: c) model elements of integrity for self- efficacy

## Introduction
A device can help you learn a prayer or find a map. It can also be used to copy, to insult, or to pretend you are someone else. Integrity includes the way your fingers behave on a screen.

## Notes
### Responsible use
- Do not copy homework from a website or from a friend and pretend you wrote it. A search can teach you; it should not do your thinking for you.
- Do not use another person's phone, password or account. A password is a key, not a toy.
- Do not send a message that you would be ashamed to say in front of a parent. Unkind words online are still your words.
- Do not photograph a classmate for a joke, and do not share their picture without permission.
- Do not click 'buy' or give a home address. Tell an adult about any message that asks for money, photos or secrecy.
- If a page is cruel about a faith, leave it and tell the teacher. Do not spread it.

### Digital citizenship
Citizenship here means you are a member of a community even when the community is on a screen. Members do not vandalise, do not steal and do not lie about their names in order to trap someone. A fake name used to harm a classmate is a serious break of integrity.

### When you make a mistake
If you posted something unkind, apologise to the person, remove it if you can, and tell an adult. Deleting it quietly without an apology is only half honest. If someone else is being targeted, do not join in. Show the message to a trusted adult instead of forwarding it.

Technology is a tool. Integrity decides whether the tool builds trust or breaks it.

## Key words
• password — a secret code that opens a device or an account
• digital citizenship — using technology in a way that is honest and fair to other people

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A classmate's homework is visible on a shared tablet. You could copy it before they return. What does integrity require?

Working:
1. The work belongs to the classmate.
2. Copying it is both stealing and lying.
3. You look away, or you close the screen, and you do your own work.

Answer: Do not read or copy their work. Complete your own.

## Activity: Honest and dishonest uses of a device
You will need: Two columns on the board, Example cards
1. Sort example cards into honest use and dishonest use. Include copying work, asking a parent before a download, sharing a cruel post, and using a map with the teacher.
2. Discuss how integrity guides the honest column.
3. Write three personal rules for devices.
4. Role-play telling an adult about a message that asks you to keep a secret.

## Practice
1. Why is copying an essay from the internet a failure of integrity?
2. What should you do if a message asks you for a photo and tells you not to tell your parents?
3. Name one honest way to use a digital device for learning.

## Summary
• Do not copy, do not use another person's password, and do not send unkind messages.
• Tell an adult about requests for money, photos or secrecy.
• Online words count as much as spoken words.

### Answers to practice
1. You are pretending that someone else's words are your own.
2. Do not send the photo. Tell a parent or teacher at once.
3. Any one: watch a lesson the teacher chose, find a map with an adult, or type your own sentences.

studyPages.title: Lesson 6: A lost and found corner
studyPages.body:
LESSON 6: A LOST AND FOUND CORNER
=================================

## What you will learn
• Explain how a lost and found corner supports integrity.
• Practise receiving and returning an item fairly.

Curriculum outcomes: c) model elements of integrity for self- efficacy; e) appreciate the value of integrity by living an exemplary life in class, school and community for harmony

## Introduction
A sweater on the field has an owner even if the owner is in another class. A lost and found corner gives integrity a place to go, so that a found item is not stuffed into a desk and forgotten.

## Notes
### How the corner works
Choose a desk, box or shelf that the whole school can understand. A found item is placed there the same day, or handed to the teacher on duty. Money should go straight to a teacher, not into an open box. Valuable items such as watches or spectacles should also go to an adult at once.

The owner describes the item before taking it. This stops a greedy person from claiming everything. Write a simple list if the teacher asks: date, item, who found it, who collected it. The list itself must be honest.

### Your part
If you find a pencil, a bottle or a jumper, you do not keep it because 'finders keepers' sounds catchy. That saying is not sadachaar. Pick the item up, ask nearby if someone just dropped it, and if not, take it to the corner or the teacher.

If you lose something, check the corner before accusing a classmate of theft. False accusations also break integrity.

### An exemplary class
A class becomes exemplary when this habit is normal. Younger learners copy what they see. If Grade 4 learners return items, they teach the school without a long speech. Include everyone: a learner who cannot walk to the field can still record items at the desk.

Harmony grows when people trust that their property is safe. Trust is the fruit of many small honest acts.

## Key words
• lost and found — a place where found items are kept until the owner collects them
• exemplary — good enough to be an example for others

## Worked examples

### Example 1
You find a named water bottle after games. A friend says, 'It has no name I recognise; let us use it.' What should you do?

Working:
1. A bottle someone carried to school is not abandoned treasure.
2. Take it to the lost and found or the teacher.
3. Using it yourself breaks asteya and school trust.

Answer: Hand the bottle to the teacher or place it in the lost and found corner.

## Activity: Set up a lost and found corner
You will need: A labelled box or desk, Paper for a record
1. With the teacher, choose a safe corner and make a clear label.
2. Role-play finding a book, recording it, and returning it only when the owner describes it.
3. Agree special rules: money and valuable items go to an adult immediately.
4. Teach the rules to another group, including any classmate who needs the steps repeated slowly.

## Practice
1. What should you do with a sweater you find on the field?
2. Why should found money not be left in an open box?
3. Why is it wrong to accuse a classmate of stealing before you check the lost and found?

## Summary
• Found items go to a lost and found corner or to a teacher.
• Money and valuable items go straight to an adult.
• A class that returns property becomes an example for the school.

### Answers to practice
1. Ask nearby if it was just dropped, and if not, take it to the lost and found corner or a teacher.
2. Money is easily taken. An adult should receive it so that it can be returned honestly.
3. The item may simply be lost, and a false accusation is unjust.

studyPages.title: Lesson 7: Practices of a passenger
studyPages.body:
LESSON 7: PRACTICES OF A PASSENGER
==================================

## What you will learn
• State safe ways to board and alight from a vehicle.
• Explain how integrity appears in the way a passenger behaves.

Curriculum outcomes: d) State ideal practices of a passenger during boarding and alighting for safety

## Introduction
A vehicle that is still moving is not a playground. Boarding and alighting are moments when carelessness causes real injury. Good passengers are also honest passengers: they pay, they queue, and they do not shove a smaller child aside.

## Notes
### Before you board
- Wait until the vehicle has fully stopped.
- Queue. Do not push, and do not climb through a window.
- Let a younger child, an older person or a person who needs help board without being crushed. Help a classmate with special needs if they ask or if a teacher asks you.
- Have your fare ready if you are paying. Do not pretend you have already paid.
- Do not board a vehicle a parent has not allowed, and do not go with a stranger who offers a free ride.

### While you are inside
- Sit properly. Do not stand on the seat or lean out of the door.
- Keep hands, head and any sticks inside.
- Do not distract the driver with shouts or by grabbing the steering area.
- Give a seat to someone who needs it more if you can stand safely, and do not spread bags over empty seats while people are standing.
- Do not drop litter or damage the fittings. The vehicle is not yours to spoil.

### Alighting
- Wait until the vehicle stops.
- Use the door. Do not jump.
- Step away from the road, not into traffic.
- Check that a younger sibling is with you before the vehicle moves off.
- If your stop is missed, speak calmly to the conductor. Do not pull at the driver.

### Integrity on the journey
Paying the correct fare, not using a forged excuse, and not destroying property are integrity. Safety rules are integrity too, because showing off at the door risks other people's bodies. A passenger who keeps these practices protects the whole vehicle.

## Key words
• board — to get onto a vehicle
• alight — to get off a vehicle
• fare — the money paid for the journey

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The bus is still rolling when friends start to jump off so they can be first at the gate. What are the safe and honest actions?

Working:
1. Alight only after the bus stops.
2. Use the door and move away from traffic.
3. Pushing to be first risks a fall and is unfair to smaller learners.

Answer: Wait for the stop, use the door, and walk clear of the road without pushing.

## Activity: Passenger checklist
You will need: Paper, A few chairs set in a row to represent seats
1. In groups, prepare a list of ideal practices for boarding and for alighting. Include safety and fair behaviour.
2. Act the correct way, then pause and point out a dangerous mistake such as jumping from a moving vehicle.
3. Add one rule about helping a passenger who needs more time.
4. Post the list in the classroom and read it before the next school trip.

## Practice
1. When is it safe to board or alight?
2. Name two dangerous passenger habits.
3. How does paying the correct fare show integrity?

## Summary
• Board and alight only when the vehicle has stopped.
• Queue, pay the fare, and do not lean out or distract the driver.
• Help passengers who need more time, and keep clear of traffic.

### Answers to practice
1. Only after the vehicle has completely stopped.
2. Any two: jumping off a moving vehicle, leaning out, distracting the driver, pushing in the queue, climbing through the window.
3. You are not cheating the conductor or taking a journey you have not paid for.

studyPages.title: Lesson 8: An exemplary life at school and beyond
studyPages.body:
LESSON 8: AN EXEMPLARY LIFE AT SCHOOL AND BEYOND
================================================

## What you will learn
• Plan how to practise integrity in class, at school and in the community.
• Appreciate integrity by encouraging others without pride.

Curriculum outcomes: c) model elements of integrity for self- efficacy; e) appreciate the value of integrity by living an exemplary life in class, school and community for harmony

## Introduction
One honest act is good. A life of integrity is a pattern that classmates can recognise over weeks. This last lesson turns the stories, the money rules, the device rules and the passenger rules into a way of belonging with other people.

## Notes
### In class
Do your own work. If you do not know an answer, say so and ask. Do not hide a group mistake inside one quiet person's name. Share materials you were given for everyone. When you mark a friend's book, mark what is truly there.

### In the wider school
Use the lost and found corner. Play games fairly. Speak about other faiths, including your own, without lies or mockery. If you are chosen as a leader, do not take food or money meant for the class. Leadership is a test of integrity, not a prize of extra power.

### In the community
Queue for water or for a vehicle. Return extra change. Point out a danger instead of daring a younger child to try it. If an adult asks you to lie for them, tell a trusted teacher or parent. A child is not required to join someone else's dishonesty.

### Harmony
The outcome of all this is harmony: people can relax because they are not waiting to be cheated. Harmony is not the silence of fear. It is the peace of fair treatment. Stories of Harishchandra, of asteya, of truthful friends and of Bhai Lalo all aim at that peace.

### Without pride
An exemplary learner does not announce, 'I am better than all of you.' Pride spoils the example. If someone fails, help them start again. If you fail, begin again the same day. Write a short essay at home: one story from a faith, one element of integrity, and one habit you will keep. That essay is a promise you can actually fulfil.

## Key words
• harmony — living together in fairness and peace
• habit — an action repeated until it becomes part of your character

## Worked examples

### Example 1
You are the class monitor. Two friends ask you to ignore their copied homework. What keeps both integrity and friendship healthy?

Working:
1. Ignoring the copy would misuse the monitor's trust.
2. You can refuse without insulting them.
3. They should redo the work. You can explain the lesson later if they ask.

Answer: Refuse to ignore the copying, speak respectfully, and let the true work be done.

## Activity: Essay on one habit of integrity
You will need: Exercise book
1. Choose one parable from the four faiths and one element of integrity it teaches.
2. Write a short essay linking that element to class, school or community.
3. Read a few essays aloud. Thank each reader.
4. Peer-teach the main lesson of your parable to a classmate who needs it repeated.

## Practice
1. Give one example of integrity in the classroom and one in the community.
2. Why does pride weaken an otherwise good example?
3. What is the link between integrity and harmony?

## Summary
• Integrity at school means honest work, fair leadership and returned property.
• Integrity in the community means fair queues, honest money and safe choices.
• The aim is harmony, practised without pride.

### Answers to practice
1. Class: doing your own work or not blaming the wrong person. Community: returning extra change, queueing fairly, or not lying for someone.
2. Boasting turns honesty into a performance and can shame other people instead of helping them.
3. When people tell the truth and do not cheat, others can trust them, and life together becomes more peaceful.

questions.question: Integrity means
options: Doing right only when a teacher is watching
Being honest even when nobody is watching
questions.explanation: Integrity is honesty that does not depend on an audience.

questions.question: King Harishchandra is remembered because he
options: Taught passengers to jump from buses
questions.explanation: His parable is about truthfulness under severe testing.

questions.question: The story of Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago teaches that
options: Honest earning is pure, and wealth gained by oppressing others is not
questions.explanation: Guru Nanak contrasted honest work with cruel profit.

questions.question: Which action shows integrity among peers?
options: Admitting a foul in a game
Hiding a group's mistake on a quiet classmate
Keeping a found watch in your bag
questions.explanation: Owning a fault is an element of integrity classmates can see.

questions.question: A shopkeeper gives you too much change. You should
options: Share it as a gift to friends
questions.explanation: Extra change is not yours. Integrity returns it.

questions.question: Which use of a device shows integrity?
options: Copying an essay and putting your name on it
Typing your own work and telling an adult about a cruel message
Posting a classmate's photo as a joke
questions.explanation: Honest work and reporting harm are responsible digital citizenship.

questions.question: A found pencil should be
options: Taken to the lost and found or a teacher
questions.explanation: A lost and found corner helps property return to the owner.

questions.question: When should a passenger alight?
options: While the vehicle is still moving, if they are late
Only after the vehicle has stopped, using the door and moving clear of traffic
questions.explanation: Boarding and alighting safely means waiting for a full stop.

questions.question: Paying the correct fare shows integrity because
questions.answer: You are not cheating the conductor or taking a journey you have not paid for.
questions.explanation: Honesty with the fare is part of a passenger's good conduct.

questions.question: An exemplary learner practises integrity in order to
options: Boast that they are better than everyone
Build trust and harmony at school and in the community
questions.explanation: The aim is a trustworthy life, not pride.
